extracted.intended_audience: health and medical journalists/reporters who cover scientific studies
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for journalists on how to evaluate, negotiate, and respond to journal and society embargo policies when covering embargoed medical research and conference releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the purpose of embargoes
rubrics_metrics.description: Embargoes are used by journals and societies to release material to reporters on a timed basis, punctuating the scientific process with 'news events.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that many outlets rely on journals for peer-reviewed findings and that synchronized releases create the weekly pattern of study coverage. Treat embargoes as part of the information-flow control that journals use, not merely a convenience for reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware embargoes can discourage original reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Embargoes may make journalists lazy, 'always chasing that week's big studies' and afraid to divert attention to more original reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the big-picture effects of accepting embargoes on your beat; don't let journal-driven news events crowd out enterprise reporting. Editors may pressure you to cover the same studies everyone else covers—push back when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the Ingelfinger Rule and its implications
rubrics_metrics.description: The Ingelfinger Rule (originating at NEJM) says journals will reject papers if their findings have been reported by the media first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the journal enforces this rule because it can limit your ability to report prior to publication. Factor this into decisions about publishing preprints, conference reporting, or breaking embargoes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect wide inconsistency across journals and societies
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals and societies handle embargoes and broken-embargo responses differently—some are consistent (e.g., JAMA, Nature group), others are not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn individual journal/society policies rather than assuming standard practice; examples include refusal to lift embargoes after breaches, extremely short embargo windows, or embargoing already-published material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for problematic embargo mechanics (local-time lifts, already-published material)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some journals set embargoes that lift at a reporter's local time (giving regional advantages) or embargo materials that are already published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to time-zone-based embargo lifts that favor certain outlets and to cases where the embargoed material is effectively public; both are signs to question the policy or push back publicly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the potential penalties for breaking embargoes
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters who publish stories before embargoes lift can be punished, for example by losing access to future materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh the costs of breaking an embargo (access loss, relationship damage) versus the public-interest value of reporting earlier; use this in editorial decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: You can't embargo something already in the public domain
rubrics_metrics.description: You can't embargo something that is already in the public domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before accepting an embargo, verify that the material is not already publicly available (e.g., posted online, presented elsewhere). If it is public, the embargo is invalid and can be challenged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiate or discuss problematic embargoes with institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes it works to discuss the policy with the embargoing institution and get them to change it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an embargo seems restrictive or unreasonable, raise the concern with the institution or journal contact. Provide reasons why the embargo harms reporting or is inconsistent; some institutions will amend policies after discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Escalate to peers, watchdogs, or professional groups when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: If discussion fails, contact watchdogs or professional organizations (e.g., Embargo Watch, Association of Health Care Journalists) to publicize or challenge restrictive policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bloggers, editors, and professional associations to expose and pressure institutions with problematic embargo rules. The author cites successfully prompting societies to change policies by publicizing issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question extremely short embargo windows
rubrics_metrics.description: Some journals (notably NEJM) insist on 'ridiculously short embargoes,' calling into question whether the policy helps journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a short embargo genuinely aids reporting or merely serves the journal's control. If it hinders responsible coverage, raise the issue with editors or consider alternative reporting strategies.
